about: Paviken (the lagoon harbour at Västergarn, west Gotland), one port, written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/paviken.md. A draft for the user to overwrite. Every person here is invented: not one name survives from this harbour. The name Paviken itself is modern. (?) = not checked on a page that was opened; late = written 150 years or more after the event.

ports.summary: A beach harbour on the east shore of a still lagoon on the west coast of Gotland, reached from the sea by one narrow strait: boats drawn up on shingle, hearths where beads, bronze and silver are worked, and men mending hulls with iron rivets. The island has no king, no town and no toll man; the farmers behind the beach are its merchants, and a stranger pays nobody but the farmer whose shore he lies on. A merchant comes for beads, combs, cast bronze and silver rings, for a boat mended or a new one laid down, and to learn how silver is weighed, because here no coin has a name.
ports.seasons: The lagoon has no tide and freezes in winter, so nothing floats from the hard frosts until the ice goes. Boats go out when the water opens and the east-farers are away all summer; the silver they bring comes home between midsummer and the first frost, and that is when the weighing shore is busiest. No fair or feast of the harbour's own is recorded.

history.text: A harbour and working ground is begun in the 700s on the east shore of the lagoon, where the stream runs in. One posthole of a gravel-floored shelter on the beach is of this century.
history.source: sv.wikipedia 'Paviken' (after P. Lundström); Länsstyrelsen i Gotlands län, 'Paviken' (archived 2011); Gotland Archaeological Field School, 'Paviken'; dossier 1, 2, 5 (the year 750 stands for 'the 700s')

history.text: The harbour is one or two generations old: beads, bronze and boat-mending. No lord, reeve or toll man is named for it in any text, then or later.
From about this time the Saracens' silver reaches the Baltic and Gotland. Whole and cut pieces of it lie in Paviken's workshop ground.
history.source: Design/content/realms/sweden_gotland.md; Gotland Archaeological Field School, 'Paviken' (two pieces of Arabic silver coin in the stone-walled house); dossier 4, 5

history.text: After this year sixty-seven kilograms of silver, in two lots, are laid under the floor of a farm building at Spillings in the north-east of the island, and never fetched.
history.source: Design/content/economy/silver_coin.md (Spillings: latest coin 870/871); hoards_793.json spillings; dossier 5

history.text: Wulfstan tells King Alfred that Blekinge, Möre, Öland and Gotland belong to the Svear. It is the only dated word of the time on who holds the island.
history.source: Wulfstan's voyage in the Old English Orosius (tr. J. Ingram 1807), as given in peoples/svea_gotlandic.md 8 and texts_793.json; dossier 1, 5

history.text: Before the end of this century, by a modern guess, Avair Strabain of Alva makes the Gotlanders' agreement with the king of the Svear: sixty marks of silver a year, forty to the king and twenty to the jarl, and the Gotlanders go free of toll in the Svear's lands. He is not known ever to have stood on this beach.
history.source: Guta saga (written about 1220, late), through en.wikipedia 'Gutasaga' and 'Gutes'; the year is a guess (?); dossier 3, 4, 5

history.text: A silver arm ring, a hammer of Thor and a bronze pendant of the 900s or 1000s are lost in the northern working ground.
history.source: Gotland Archaeological Field School, 'Paviken'; dossier 5 (the year 950 stands for '900s to 1000s')

history.text: Jarl Eirik of Lade robs ships off Gotland this year and the next.
history.source: Heimskringla (tr. S. Laing 1844), late, through realms/sweden_gotland.md; dossier 3, 5

history.text: About now, if the usual date holds, a half-ring wall a thousand paces long is raised at Västergarn, on the seaward side of the lagoon's outlet. Its date is not settled, and the houses dug inside it are later.
history.source: sv.wikipedia 'Västergarnsvallen' (R. Edberg's review of D. Carlsson, Vikingatidens Västergarn, Fornvännen 2012); Länsstyrelsen, 'Västergarn Västergarnsvallen'; dossier 2, 5

history.text: About this year the boy Olaf Haraldsson of Norway takes tribute of the island.
history.source: Heimskringla (tr. Laing 1844), late, through realms/sweden_gotland.md; dossier 3, 5

history.text: Timber quays and jetties and a stone facing are built at the lagoon's outlet; the trees were felled this year. A spring flood later wrecks them.
history.source: Gotland Archaeological Field School, 'Paviken' (tree-ring date); sv.wikipedia 'Västergarnsvallen'; dossier 2, 5

history.text: In the early 1000s a row of piles is driven across the entrance to the lagoon and closes it.
history.source: sv.wikipedia 'Paviken' (after Lundström); Länsstyrelsen, 'Paviken'; dossier 2, 5 (the year stands for 'early 1000s')

history.text: Olaf Haraldsson lies at Akergarn in the north-east of the island on his way east. It is a long way from this lagoon.
An English penny of the 1030s, pierced and worn as a pendant, is lost at Västergarn.

By about now the lagoon is too shallow for laden boats: the land has risen and the stream has silted it. What trade is left is said to move to the Västergarn shore, though the finds there are thin for these years.
history.source: en.wikipedia and sv.wikipedia 'Paviken'; sv.wikipedia 'Västergarnsvallen'; the year is a fair guess (?); dossier 5, 8

eras.text: A young harbour. Eight or ten boats on the shingle in summer, a walled yard where glass is melted for beads, hearths on a floor of laid stones, and hulls propped on the beach with men under them clenching rivets. Silver is rings, bars and old brooches cut to the weight; nobody here has yet seen a white coin with writing all round it.

The east-farers come home each year between midsummer and the first frost with thin white coins, whole and cut in halves and quarters. The smith melts some into bars; most of it goes inland and is not seen again. A stone-walled store stands between the working ground and the southern graves. More boats, more scales, and the same silence about what a farm holds.

The best-off farms have more silver than they can use, and it lies under floors. Weights cut to the eastern coin's standard are common on the shore. Men from the Svear's side come to talk of a yearly payment and free passage; the beach speaks of it for years and nobody says who agreed. Strangers say the island belongs to the Svear. No Gotlander says so.

The flood of silver, then its thinning. Until about the middle of the century every boat from the east rides low; after it the coins are fewer and worse, and the smith nicks each one. Arm rings are made to a weight, a hand's worth of silver that can be worn. The lagoon is a little shallower every lifetime, and the old men say so.

Bad years on the water. A jarl from Norway robs ships off the island two summers running, and a boy king takes tribute of it. Boats are hauled higher and watched at night. No white coin has come from the east in years: what comes now is the emperor's pennies and the English king's, weighed like everything else.

The harbour is moving. Timber quays stand at the outlet, where laden boats can still lie, and a row of piles shuts the old entrance to all but those who know the gap. Across the outlet, earth is being heaped into a long curved bank. A few men come home baptised and a few bring a priest; the smith casts hammers and crosses from one stone. The old beach is for small boats and mending.

The lagoon is nearly a lake: reeds where boats were hauled, the strait a ditch a boy can wade. A few hearths still burn for beads and rivets, and the dead are still carried to the grave fields, but silver from abroad is scarce and the weighing is done on the seaward shore, behind the bank at Västergarn. A skipper who knew the old water would not find his way in.

sites.name: The dragging beach
sites.see: A long curve of pale shingle on still brown water, with a hollow worn into it where boats have been dragged up for longer than anyone remembers. Eight or ten clinker boats lie on rollers, their square sails spread to dry in chequers of two colours. Behind them stand low sheds, and behind those thin blue smoke from a dozen hearths; far across the lagoon a single gap of bright sea. Hammering, gulls, tar, and cattle lowing inland.
sites.source: A hollow worn by dragging boats at the waterfront; a sheltered lagoon joined to the sea by one narrow strait (Gotland Archaeological Field School, 'Paviken'; sv.wikipedia 'Paviken'; dossier 1). Chequered sails from Gotland's picture stones (en.wikipedia 'Picture stone'). The landing gift to the farmer whose beach it is: realms/sweden_gotland.md, 'who must be paid'. The number of boats is the game's (traffic_793.json).

sites.name: The weighing shore
sites.see: The strip of trodden ground where the stream meets the lagoon. No booths and no benches: hides spread on the stones, and on them strings of beads, combs, bronze pins, coils of rope, a heap of rivets. Every second man has a small folding balance and holds it up against the light off the water before he speaks. Behind, the stone wall of the fine-craft yard and its smoke. It is quiet for a market; the loudest thing is the stream.
sites.source: The western, waterfront part of the northern ground ('Area 1'), with the most silver and the most weights, read as the place of exchange (Gotland Archaeological Field School; dossier 2). Scale fragments, lead weights and cubo-octahedral weights (dossier 4). No coin is struck; silver is weighed (ports_793.json; npc_roles_793.json has_mint false). A Gotland farmer at the market gives a rune stick here (unlocks_793.json text.t-gest-32).

sites.name: The walled yard
sites.see: A yard inside a dry-stone wall as high as a man's chest, open on the side toward the stream. In the middle a hearth as long as a man, and beside it a low platform of baked clay with an iron rod, tongs and a row of small bright cubes laid out on it: red, yellow, a blue like deep water, a few with gold inside the glass. A man turns a rod in the flame and a bead grows on it. Lumps of dark red stone and raw amber lie in a trough. Charcoal smoke, and the hiss of hot glass in water.
sites.source: The fine-craft yard ('Area 2') inside a stone wall, opening toward the stream Idån: raw glass, raw garnet, amber, ingots; a hearth of 2 by 1 m and a clay platform perhaps used in bead-making, found 2013 (Gotland Archaeological Field School; dossier 2). Opaque glass cubes read as Italian mosaic stones (dossier 4). The height of the wall is the game's guess (?).

sites.name: The paved ground
sites.see: South of the yard the earth is laid with flat stones to make a working floor, black with soot between them. Three hearths, one roofed with turf on posts; a pit of slag and burnt bone; a stump with an iron block set in it. Two men draw rivets by the hundred and throw them hissing into a trough. Scraps of bronze and bent iron lie where they fell. It smells of hot iron and singed horn, and the hammers never keep the same time.
sites.source: The rough-work ground ('Area 3'): stone paving laid as a working floor, hearths, rubbish pits, postholes, bronze and iron scrap, much burnt bone (Gotland Archaeological Field School; dossier 2). Boat rivets and nails are found all over the site from the first test pits of 1961 (dossier 2). Comb and dice makers in bone and antler (dossier 3).

sites.name: The slip and the boat sheds
sites.see: A hull lies on the shingle with half her planks on, pale new wood over dark, each plank lapped on the one below and held by a row of rivet heads. A broad man in a leather apron sights along her with one eye shut. Beside her an old boat is propped on her side with a plank cut out. Sheds with turf roofs hold oars, moss, tar pots and a pile of roves. Adze chips underfoot, the smell of tar and split pine, the dull knock of a mallet.
sites.source: Boats were mended here: rivets and nails over the whole ground and a slipway hollow (Gotland Archaeological Field School; dossier 2). That boats were also built is usual in the books and not shown by the pages opened (?): the game lets one be laid down, as ports_793.json ('shipwrights and smiths') and story/ships_793.json (built_at) do. A Gotland shipwright sells and gives rune sticks here (unlocks_793.json text.t-gest-06, text.t-vafth-35; riddles_793.json r-gest-06, answer: the anchor).

sites.name: The stone-walled house
sites.see: A small house with walls of piled limestone and a roof of turf, standing by itself between the working ground and the southern graves. There is no hearth in it and no smoke hole: it is cold inside on the hottest day. Bales, casks and bundled skins along the walls; on a ledge a folded balance, a row of lead weights and a block of yellow sandstone with a shape cut into it. A heavy plank door with a wooden bar, and a dog asleep against it.
sites.source: The stone-walled house between the northern and southern grounds, dug 1995, of the Viking Age: no hearth; rivets, scale fragments, lead weights, glass, two pieces of Arabic silver coin, and a sandstone mould for crosses or Thor's hammers; a workshop or store, not a dwelling (Gotland Archaeological Field School; dossier 2). Its year of building is not known: 800 is the game's (?).

sites.name: The gravel-floored shelter
sites.see: A long low shelter above the tide line: posts, a roof of turf and reed, a floor of beaten gravel, three sides walled with wattle and the fourth open to the water. Sea chests and rolled sleeping skins along the back; a fire in a ring of stones at the open end with a pot over it. In the evening men sit on their chests with a board of pegged pieces between them, and somebody is always mending a net. Fish broth, wet wool, peat smoke.
sites.source: The beach house dug in 2014: a thin gravel floor and one posthole dated to the 8th century, a store or shelter (Gotland Archaeological Field School; dossier 2). Whether anyone lived at the harbour all year is not settled (dossier 1): strangers sleeping here under a farm's protection is the game's guess (?). Dice in bone and antler were made on the site (dossier 3); dice and tafl are played here (story/town_games_793.json). From 871 a skald of the Gotlanders sits here (unlocks_793.json text.t-gest-08).

sites.name: The ring of stones
sites.see: In the middle of the working ground, with hearths on every side of it, a ring of grey stones as wide as a boat is long, the grass inside it uncut. Nobody walks across it; the path bends round. On the nearest stone lie an amber bead, a lump of slag and a crust. Beside the ring a pit of ash and split cattle bone, and an iron cauldron upside down on three stones. At dusk the light comes low across the lagoon and the stones throw shadows as far as the yard wall.
sites.source: A round stone setting at the centre of the northern ground: one man buried unburnt with a ring brooch, and cremations beside him (Gotland Archaeological Field School; dossier 2). The harbour is heathen through its main life: hammers of Thor in amber and metal (dossier 6). That offerings and a shared boiled meal were made beside it is the game's guess (?): the meal and its 'boiling-fellows' are from the Guta saga (late), and the burnt bone is the rough ground's. No shrine building is known and none is shown.

sites.name: The southern graves
sites.see: A slope of short grass and juniper south of the hearths, set with low rings and heaps of stone, some sunk almost level, some new and pale. One low heap is twice as long as the rest. At the upper edge stands a slab of limestone taller than a man, narrow at the neck and wide at the head, with a ship under sail cut on it and painted red and black. A man with a mallet and a pointed iron kneels at a second slab lying flat. Wind, sheep, and the tap of iron on stone.
sites.source: The south grave field: stone settings, cremations and burials, one grave holding a dog and a horse; a further field to the south, ploughed out, perhaps hundreds of graves once (Gotland Archaeological Field School; dossier 2). Picture stones of 700 to 1100 are tall, with ships under chequered sails (en.wikipedia 'Picture stone'); none is recorded from Paviken itself, so the standing stone and the carver are invented (?) (dossier 6). The memorial stone a house can pay for is unlocks_793.json memorial_picture_stone; the carver gives rune sticks (text.t-gest-35, text.t-vafth-47).

sites.name: Aikgard, half a morning inland
sites.see: Up the stream past two fords, with a low ridge on the left hand: a long house of timber and turf, a storehouse on a stone footing, a well, and sheep on thin grass over white limestone. By the gate a tall stone with a ship cut on it. A heavy man sets bread and ale on a table by the open door and asks nothing until it is eaten. Beyond the pasture fence a row of old standing stones shows against the sky. Wind in ash trees, a dog on a rope, and a long quiet.
sites.source: Invented, for the chain dirham_hoard (Design/content/chains/dirham_hoard.md; encounters/chain_dirham_hoard_793.json): the farm, its name and its people. True to the island: farmers who are also the merchants, and silver hoards on farms, many inside the footings of houses (peoples/svea_gotlandic.md 5; economy/silver_coin.md). The thing that meets on the slope above the farms is the chain's and is not a place at the harbour. The years are the chain's window.

sites.name: The ship of stones in the east pasture
sites.see: In the pasture east of the farm, grey standing stones set in the shape of a ship, bow to the sea: the tallest at stem and stern, the rest lower amidships, all leaning and patched with yellow lichen. Sheep lie in the lee of them. The turf at the stern stone is whole. Nobody at the farm knows who raised it or for whom, only that it was old in their grandfathers' time. In the evening the stones are black against a yellow sky.
sites.source: Ship settings of standing stones are common on Gotland and were already ancient in these years (the Bronze Age settings at Gannarve and 'Tjelvar's grave'), as the chain page says (?). This one, and that silver lies in it, are invented for the chain dirham_hoard.

sites.name: The timber quays at the outlet
sites.see: Where the lagoon drains to the sea, new oak piles stand in two rows with planking on them, and the bank is faced with fitted stone. A laden boat can lie afloat here, which she no longer can at the old beach. Out in the old entrance a line of pile heads breaks the water, with one gap a boat's width across. On the seaward side men are heaping earth and stone into a long curved bank. Fresh-cut oak, wet rope, and the stream running fast under the planks.
sites.source: Timber quays and jetties and a stone facing at the outlet Västergarnsån, tree-ring dated to 1008, wrecked by a spring flood (Gotland Archaeological Field School; sv.wikipedia 'Västergarnsvallen'); a row of piles closing the entrance, early 1000s (sv.wikipedia 'Paviken'). More coins and weights near the outlet than on the northern ground: perhaps a second trading spot (dossier 2). The bank is the Västergarn wall, about 1000 if the usual date holds, and is Västergarn's, not this harbour's (dossier 2, 8). The gap in the piles is the game's guess (?). The skipper met here is the heir of the one of 793.

people.name: Rodbjorn
people.trait: The man the beach sends for when a plank is sprung. Slow to answer, exact, and unable to pass a hull without knocking on it.
people.want: To lay down one ship for the open sea before his hands stiffen, for an owner who will not tell him how to build her.
people.fear: A boat of his opening a seam off a lee shore, and the kin of four men walking down to the slip to ask why.
people.voice: Puts down his adze before he answers, and if he does not pick it up again the news is bad. Talks of boats as 'she' and of owners as weather.
people.looks: About forty-five, broad and short-legged, a brown beard with wood chips in it, a leather apron black with tar over a grey wool shirt, an adze in his hand and a bag of rivets at his belt.
knows: what any hull on the beach is worth, to an ounce, and what is wrong with her that her owner has not said
which farms inland have oak and pine standing and who will sell it
the road to every farm up the stream, and which farms are speaking to each other
the riddle of the thing that fights wave and wind and bites the ground: he sells it cut on a stick for three pennies' weight
how the Danes lay a keel, and why he thinks it wrong

ties.note: the smith draws his rivets; they have argued about the price of iron for twenty years and eaten together every midwinter
the skipper's boat was mended on a promise three summers ago; Rodbjorn has not been paid and has not asked
his sister's husband's sister; the slip stands on her farm's shore and he pays for it in mending
in the chain's years his heir at the slip knows Aikgard well: a careful farm that has not sold a sheep it could keep
a Dane who worked two winters on this slip and still lays a keel the Gutes' way
his house buys her cloth each autumn and tells her nothing about its silver
the Danes' wright at the fjord head, who builds long and narrow and says Gotland boats are tubs for sheep; each has mended the other's work and said nothing kind
Holmfast has his boat's garboards looked at here every second year and counts the rivets afterwards
Ravn once answered his anchor riddle before he had finished saying it; Rodbjorn has not forgiven him and likes him for it
a widow of his mother's kin keeps the strangers' house on the Curonian shore, three generations off; she knows the farm's name and has never seen it
in the chain's years the young steersman sits at his heir's slip on idle days and is told what is wrong with every boat but the one he wants
his son's son, who has the slip and the adze two lifetimes on, and keeps a rune stick under his keels that he takes for a charm

lines.greet: A Frisian boat. Short in the keel and full in the bow. Who built her? No, do not tell me. Let me knock on her first.
lines.greet_again: She came back, then. I looked at her from the shed when you rounded the point. The third strake on the steering side is weeping.
rumour: A Dane learned his trade on this slip and went home to Skane. He sends word when he wants rivets. He never sends word that I was right.
The lagoon is a hand shallower than when my father hauled boats here. Nobody believes me. The boats believe me.
Three boats went east this year, and I mended all three first. When they come home low I am paid. Then they forget where the silver went.
lines.saying: A boat tells you what she needs. An owner tells you what he can pay. Listen to the boat.
lines.farewell: Keep her bailed and keep her tarred. If she talks in the night, come back before she shouts.

people.source: invented. Boat-menders are shown by the rivets and nails all over the ground (Gotland Archaeological Field School, 'Paviken'; dossier 3); the role and its riddles from npc_roles_793.json (shipwright) and riddles_793.json r-gest-06. Name: Rod- (Rodvisl, G 134) + -björn (Hegbjörn, G 280), both on Gotland stones of a later century. His son and grandson keep the slip after him.

people.name: Hegvisl
people.trait: Bead-maker, bronze-caster and pourer of silver bars, in that order of pride. Patient with fire and short with people who hurry him.
people.want: Glass of the bright colours, the small cubes that come up from the south: the red, the yellow, and above all the ones with gold shut inside.
people.fear: A bar of his found light or mixed with tin, and his mark worth nothing on any beach from here to the Danes.
people.voice: Speaks to the fire, not to you. Names a weight, never a price, and lets you work out the rest.
people.looks: About forty, lean and stooped, a singed fair beard, burn scars on both forearms, a wool cap, a leather apron, an iron rod with a blob of red glass on its end.
knows: what your penny weighs, and what is in it besides silver
how to nick, bend and ring a piece of silver to try it, and what each mark on an old piece means
who on the beach holds raw amber, garnet or scrap bronze this week
that the bright glass cubes are prised out of walls far to the south, and that he does not care whose walls
which buyers at Birka and on the Danes' river want beads, and which want only the glass

ties.note: draws his rivets and argues the price of iron with him every year
each says the other's work is only patience; each has the other's work in his house
melts the skipper's eastern silver into bars and rings and is told nothing of where the rest goes
in the chain's years the smith at this hearth makes her weights and thinks her the best eye for silver on the shore
he learned the sprung pin on a plot at the Danes' river market and brought it home; the Dane who showed him still wants paying
the last caster on the Svear's holy island; they met once at Birka and compared weights for half a day
Toki, a bead-maker of the Danes' west market, who buys the same glass cubes from Frisians and outbids him
Ragnvi of Birka winds beads as he does and sends him her failed colours to guess at
Holmfast buys his beads by the hundred string to take east and weighs every string
the smith on the eastern river is of his father's brother's line; a Gute skipper carries word between the two forges every second summer

lines.greet: Put your silver on the pan, not in my hand. I do not know your king. I know what he weighs.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian with the heavy pennies. Good silver, your king's. A pity he spoils it with his name. What did you bring me that is not silver?
rumour: The bright cubes come from the south, out of old walls. Some have gold shut in the glass. I melt them. A bead is worth more than a wall.
A Svea paid me in a half coin last autumn, white, with writing round it like ants. Good silver. Better than yours, and no king on it at all.
The amber is poor this year. The Este are keeping the big pieces for somebody. Ask at their lake market who it is, and tell me.
lines.saying: Silver has one name, and it is its weight.
lines.farewell: Bring glass. Red and yellow, and the gold kind if you can find it. I pay in beads or in knowing, whichever you are short of.

people.source: invented. Bead-makers, bronze-casters and silversmiths casting bars are shown by the finds: raw glass cubes, raw garnet, amber, ingots, a mould for silver bars (Gotland Archaeological Field School, 'Paviken'; dossier 3, 4). His weighing of the stranger's penny is the spine's hook for this port (silver_road: sets sv_scale). Name: Heg- (Hegbjörn, G 280) + -visl (Rodvisl, G 134). His heirs keep the hearth.

people.name: Botbjorn
people.trait: A farmer with forty sheep who is at sea from the going of the ice to the first frost. Easy, lucky, and closed like a chest about what he owns.
people.want: Things the east will pay for and the west makes: Rhine blades, glass, good cloth. And a buyer in the west who does not ask where the furs came from.
people.fear: The year his luck is used up; and his neighbours learning how much is under his floor before his sons are grown.
people.voice: Cheerful about everything except his own affairs. Answers a question about silver with a question about the weather.
people.looks: About thirty-five, long and loose-limbed, sun-bleached hair tied back, a short fair beard, a sea-stained blue cloak with a ring pin, a silver arm ring pushed high under the sleeve, a round bronze scale case at his belt.
knows: the crossing to the Curonian shore and to the Este, and the way north to the Svear's lake
what furs, wax and people fetch at the river mouth in the east, as of last autumn
which Gotland boats went east this year and which are not home
where on the west coast of the island a boat can run in from a north wind
what was paid at Birka for Rhine glass, if you ask him twice

ties.note: three summers' mending on a promise; he means to pay when the next boat comes home full
brings him the white silver to melt, a little at a time
her brother's son; he hauls out on her shore and brings her a marten skin each autumn for it
in the chain's years the skipper of this house is the young man's foster-father at sea, and says he steers better than he reckons
the pilots at the Danes' river mouth in Skane, down to Asgot in the house's later days: the skippers of this house cross that bar without them, and say so to their faces
a dealer at the river town in the east who keeps the dark sables back for him and wants swords for them
old Botgair, his father's cousin, keeps the Gotlanders' store on the Curonian shore; he sleeps at that fire on the way east and carries its news home
they buy from the same men in the east; Holmfast weighs three times and Botbjorn once, and each thinks the other a fool
sold him the cut white coin the Wend wears on a thong, for a joke and a cask of honey
Likbjorn has promised him a stone with a fat boat on it, low in the water; he says there is no hurry
the Curonian who has brought him in over the bar eleven springs running; they share no tongue and get on well
the big man on the eastern river would like to know what the Gotlanders carry home; Botbjorn sells at the blanket and tells him about the weather
the pilot of the eastern river brings him over the lake without a Svea aboard, and is paid in salt
Hailgair has witnessed his oath at the ring before three sailings; a thing sworn there needs no stick

lines.greet: A boat from the Rhine mouth on this beach. You are either lost or clever. Sit down and tell me which.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian. Good. I told my wife you would come back, and she said no man sails that far twice for beads.
rumour: There is a town on a river in the east where a sword buys more furs than the boat will hold. I am not telling you which river.
The Svea Holmfast weighed my wax three times at Birka. I asked whether it had grown. He weighed it again.
Two boats from the north of the island are not home, and the nights are drawing in. Nobody says anything yet. We do not say it until the frost.
lines.saying: Ask a Gute what he has and he will tell you about his sheep.
lines.farewell: Fair wind. If you meet a Wend with a white coin round his neck, tell him the man who sold it wants more of that honey.

people.source: invented. The island's farmers are its merchants (realms/sweden_gotland.md; peoples/svea_gotlandic.md 1); the eastern silver comes home between midsummer and the first frost (economy/silver_coin.md); the spine's hook: 'men who sail east each summer and come home with silver they put under the floor and never speak of'. Name: Bot- (Botair, Guta saga) + -björn. His son keeps the boat after him, and his son's sons are met at the outlet quays after 1008.

people.name: Rodiaud
people.trait: The widow whose farm owns the beach. She takes the landing gift, says where a stranger sleeps, and answers for him while he sleeps there.
people.want: Salt, wine and good cloth without crossing the sea for them; and guests who make no trouble she must pay for.
people.fear: A stranger under her roof killing or being killed, and her farm paying a man's price before the neighbours.
people.voice: Hospitable and blunt. Feeds you first and tells you the rules while you are chewing.
people.looks: About fifty, straight-backed, grey hair under a linen cloth, a brown strap dress held by two round box brooches with strings of glass and amber beads between them, keys and a small knife at her belt.
knows: whose shore each stretch of the beach is, and what gift each farm expects
that an outlander's life is priced at ten marks here and a Gotlander's at twenty-four, and what follows from that
who is in harbour, who left, and what they would not say they carried
the old tales of the island: that it sank by day until fire was brought to it
which crewman of yours was loud in the shelter last night

ties.note: her brother's son; she thinks he has more luck than sense and keeps his sea chest when he is ashore
kin by marriage; the slip is on her shore
she has ordered her husband's stone and paid half; he has cut the ship and not yet the rider
in the chain's years the widow of the three ash trees is of this farm's kin: the house Ailikn went back to
Fastlög's house at Birka lodges her kin and is lodged here in turn; each sends the other cloth and cheese it thinks is better
Holmfast sleeps in her shelter and pays in salt, weighed, which she pretends to find insulting
Ravn has slept here before and knows to bring the gift to the door himself and not send a boy
the farmer who says the law at the ring; he names the gift a stranger owes her shore, and she collects it

lines.greet: You are on my shore. That is no complaint. Bring something to the door, eat what you are given, and you are my guest and not a stranger.
lines.greet_again: The same boat, and the same man with the big laugh in it. He sleeps at the far end this time. You are welcome. Come and eat.
rumour: A stranger's life is ten marks here and one of ours twenty-four. I did not make the sum. Stay near my fire and nobody has to do it.
They say this island sank under the sea every morning until a man carried fire onto it. I have a nephew like that. He needs watching by day.
There is no toll man. People come from the Franks' rivers and look round for one as if they had lost a dog.
lines.saying: A guest brings his gift to the door and his knife no further.
lines.farewell: Go well. The shelter is yours when you come again, and the gift is the same. I do not raise it for friends, or forget it for them.

people.source: invented. No ruler, reeve or toll is recorded for the harbour (dossier 1, 4); on Gotland a stranger pays 'the farmer whose beach it is, and nobody else' and needs a host who answers for him (realms/sweden_gotland.md; peoples/svea_gotlandic.md 12). Wergild of ten and twenty-four marks from the Guta Lag (about 1220, late). The sinking island from the Guta saga (late). Women run farms and hold silver (peoples/svea_gotlandic.md 3). Name: Rodiaud, on a Gotland stone, G 111 (?). Her farm's daughters keep the shore after her.

people.name: Likbjorn
people.trait: Cuts and paints the tall stones for the dead. Has thought about death longer than most men and finds it mainly a matter of measurement.
people.want: To be asked for something other than a ship and a rider. Once, anything else: a smith, a woman weaving, a Frisian with a short cloak.
people.fear: His eyes. He holds the stone closer each year and cuts by touch more than he admits.
people.voice: Dry, slow, and fond of a riddle. Speaks of the dead in the present and of his customers in the past.
people.looks: About fifty-five, thin and grey, stone dust in his beard and brows, a patched undyed tunic, knees wrapped in sheepskin, a wooden mallet and a pointed iron, red ochre under his nails.
knows: who lies under each ring of stones on the slope, and who paid for the stone and who did not
what the pictures on a stone mean: the ship, the rider, the woman with the horn, the horse with too many legs
sixteen runes, and how to cut a line of them round an edge
the question of who goes over the ground and swallows wood and water, and several others he gives away for nothing
which men went east and are remembered here with no bones under the stone

ties.note: says the smith makes things that are lost in a year; the smith says his are at least looked at
is cutting her husband's stone, slowly, because she paid half
has promised him a stone with a fat boat on it, low in the water; the skipper says there is no hurry
in the chain's years the carver on this slope cut the stone by Aikgard's gate, and knows which brother paid for it
the Svear king's skald trades him verses for riddles; neither will say who is ahead
Grimulf of Birka came one summer to learn what the pictures on the stones are said to mean, and went home with three different answers
Ravn sets him a riddle each time and has never had the same answer back twice
Hailgair says the words over his customers at the ring for nothing; Likbjorn cut his father's stone and was paid in full, which he likes to mention

lines.greet: A living man. They are rarer up here than you would think. Mind the slab, it is somebody's father.
lines.greet_again: You again, and still alive. I had half a mind to start on your ship. What does she carry at the stern, so that I get it right?
rumour: A woman ordered a stone for a son who went east. No body. I cut the ship a little smaller when there is no body. Nobody has noticed.
The horse has eight legs because it is fast, or because four men carry a bier. I have been told both by people who were sure.
A skipper asked me for a stone with silver on it. I said the whole island knows about your silver. He went pale. It was a joke.
lines.saying: Every man gets a ship in the end. Some get one they can sail.
lines.farewell: Come back and tell me how the Franks mark their dead. If it is a pile of stones with a stick on it, I do not want to know.

people.source: invented. No picture stone is recorded from Paviken itself; stones stand in neighbouring parishes (?) (dossier 6). The pictures from en.wikipedia 'Picture stone' and lore/gods_cult.md (Tängelgårda, Ardre, Lärbro: a ship under sail, a rider met by a woman with a horn, a horse with eight legs; the names given to the scenes are later). The role and his riddles from riddles_793.json ('a Gotland stone-carver', 793-1066) and unlocks_793.json memorial_picture_stone. Name: Lik- (Liknat, G 113) + -björn. A carver works this slope in every generation.

people.name: Hailgair
people.trait: A farmer of the west shore who says the law at the ring of stones when the farms meet: he has it by heart, and says it at one speed whoever is listening.
people.want: That strangers learn the one rule before they need it: on this island a guest pays the farmer whose shore he lies on, and that farmer answers for him.
people.fear: A dispute over buried silver. Every farm has some, nobody admits to any, and the law has no words for what is not there.
people.voice: Level and unhurried. Says a thing once, in the order the law has it, and then waits as long as it takes.
people.looks: Near fifty in 793, broad and weathered, a grey beard cut square, a brown wool cloak pinned at the shoulder with a plain bronze ring-pin, a farmer's hands, and a staff he does not lean on.
knows: what a stranger owes the shore he lands on, and who answers for him if he does harm
what is sworn at the ring of stones, and which oaths were kept
which farms sent boats east this year, though not what they brought home
what a man's life is priced at, and that a stranger's is priced lower (the law as later written; here by custom) (?)
that the Svear ask what the island pays for its own law, and what he answers

ties.note: the Svear's lawman at the kings' mounds asked him what the Gotlanders pay to say their own law; he answered: nothing yet
names the gift a stranger owes her shore when she asks him to, and has never had to name it twice
has witnessed his oath at the ring before three sailings, and the reckoning after two of them
the stone-cutter cut his father's stone; he says the words over the carver's customers for nothing

lines.greet: A stranger on Rodiaud's shore. Then she answers for you, and you answer to her. That is the whole of the law you need today.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian. Nobody has brought me a complaint with your name in it. I say so because you would not otherwise hear.
rumour: A Svea lawman asked me what we pay their king to say our own law. I said: nothing yet. He wrote nothing down. They do not write either.
A thing sworn at the ring is known to every farm by evening. That is why nobody here cuts a stick for it.
Two farms are quarrelling over a boundary stone. Neither will say what lies under it. I cannot judge what nobody will name.
lines.saying: The law is short. It is the remembering that takes a lifetime.
lines.farewell: Go well. If you come back with a quarrel, bring it to the ring and not to the beach.

people.source: invented: the 'paviken.lawman' of uppsalir.holmgeir's tie. No ruler, reeve or toll is recorded for the harbour (dossier paviken); the Gotlanders' own law and thing, a stranger's lower price and the host who answers for a guest are from the Guta law as written down about 1220 (LATER; realms/sweden_gotland.md, peoples/svea_gotlandic.md), here as custom. That the island paid the Svear king a yearly tax for peace is the Guta saga's tale of a later agreement (?): in 793 he can still say 'nothing yet'. Name: Hail- + -gair, both on Gotland rune stones (?). A farmer says the law at the ring in every generation.

people.name: Vivil
people.trait: The elder brother who holds the farm Aikgard. Careful to the point of pain: he has not sold a sheep he could keep in twenty years.
people.want: The farm whole, its silver in the ground where no one can spend it, and no stranger's name in his family's business.
people.fear: That his brother's daughter will carry the farm's silver to another roof; and that he is sicker than he says.
people.voice: Few words, eyes on the table. Feeds a guest fully before he asks one question, and then asks the only one that matters.
people.looks: About fifty, heavy, a grey-brown beard, a farmer's undyed tunic and a good belt, earth on both knees, a spade never far from the door post.
knows: the law of a farm as the island keeps it: brothers hold it together, the eldest speaks, land does not leave the kin
that there is silver in his dead brother's storehouse, and not where
every boundary stone of Aikgard and who moved one in his father's time
when the thing meets on the slope, and who knows the law by heart

ties.note: his brother's daughter; each claims the whole of what her father left, and they agree only on the day to lift the floor
a young man of the Aikgard kin who wants a ship; Vivil thinks a ship is a hole in the water you pour silver into
the wright of the day points strangers up the stream to his farm, and puts down his adze first
the stone by his gate was his brother's order; the second half of the price is still talked about
if his brother Hegbjorn died at the Danes' fjord market: the ale-house that nursed him through his last fever and saw him burned decently

lines.greet: Eat first. There is bread and there is ale. Whatever you came up the stream to say will keep until the bowl is empty.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian. The dog knew your step. Sit. I will say this once: you carried a hard word honestly, and I do not forget either half of that.
rumour: My brother went east thirty summers. He brought home silver and put it where the sheep could not eat it. That is all I ever asked of him.
A farm is not cut up. Cut a farm in two and you have two men who cannot feed a horse.
They want a ship. A ship comes home or does not. A hole in the ground has never once been lost off the Curonian shore.
lines.saying: What is in the ground is not in anybody's mouth.
lines.farewell: You know the path. Keep the ridge on your right hand going down. And stay out of the east pasture unless I am with you.

people.source: invented, for the chain dirham_hoard (Design/content/chains/dirham_hoard.md; writing/chain_dirham_hoard.json): this entry follows the chain's words and must not be read against them. He is alive in whatever year the chain is played (805 to 949), so no birth year is given. Name: Vivil, on the Pilgårds stone, G 280 (later). Inheritance custom from the Guta Lag (about 1220, late), used for colour only (?).

people.name: Ailikn
people.trait: The dead east-farer's only child: widowed two winters, one small boy, living with her mother's people under three ash trees near the shore. She asks her uncle for nothing.
people.want: What her father meant her to have, counted aloud before witnesses; and then to put it to work, a shore strip and half a ship.
people.fear: Her boy growing up a guest on other people's farms.
people.voice: Quiet and exact. Cuts a notch for every mark weighed and trusts the stick over anyone's memory, her own included.
people.looks: About twenty-six, spare and upright, fair hair under a widow's cloth, a grey strap dress with plain bronze brooches, a tally stick and a small knife at her belt, a boy of four holding her skirt.
knows: that her father once walked her to a stone and said nothing there
how to weigh silver and keep a tally, better than most skippers
what a shore strip at the harbour costs and which farm would sell one
what the west wants from the east and what it pays, from every skipper she has ever listened to

ties.note: her father's brother; she does not hate him, which makes it harder
kin of her own age; if there is ever a ship, he steers and she tallies
the farm of the three ash trees is of the beach widow's kin and took her back
the smith of her day pours her weights and says she has the best eye for silver on the shore
if the chain is played in Catla's years: a Svea woman at Birka who also carries a dead parent's silver, and understood her at once

lines.greet: You are the one who was with my father at the end. Tell me how he was first. The rest I can wait for.
lines.greet_again: The boy asks after your boat. He has decided it is his. I told him a boat is a third share at the least.
rumour: My father took me to an old stone when I was nine and stood there. He said nothing. I thought he was tired. I think about it now.
My uncle would bury silver, then bury the spade. He is not a bad man. He is a man who has never lost anything and means not to begin.
A skipper told me Rhine wine sells for twice its weight in wax at the eastern river town. I cut that on a stick. I keep such sticks.
lines.saying: Silver in the ground feeds nobody. It does not even feed the worms.
lines.farewell: Any winter you are caught in these waters, the three ash trees. I do not say that to be kind. I say it so that you know where.

people.source: invented, for the chain dirham_hoard; this entry follows the chain's words. She is alive in whatever year the chain is played (805 to 949). A woman with silver of her own is true to the time: Frideburg and Catla of Birka (Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 20, tr. Robinson 1921); women who raise stones and hold farms (peoples/svea_gotlandic.md 3). Name: Ailikn, on a Gotland stone, G 114 (?).

people.name: Ottar
people.trait: A young man of the Aikgard kin who has steered other men's boats east four summers and wants one of his own. Open-faced, for a Gotlander.
people.want: A ship built on this beach, a hold full of what the east wants, and partners who will leave their share in her.
people.fear: Ending as his uncle did: rich, far from home, with strangers at the bedside.
people.voice: Quick and warm until silver is named. Then he remembers where he is from and says half as much.
people.looks: About twenty-four, tall, wind-reddened, a short fair beard, a salt-stained wool tunic and sealskin shoes, a steering thong wound round one wrist, hands harder than his years.
knows: the east road as far as the river town and one river beyond it
what a new ship costs at the slip, and how long the wright would take
which men of the beach would row for a share and which only for pay
what his uncle Hegbjorn used to carry east, and that he never said what he brought back

ties.note: the head of his kin's farm, who thinks ships are for other men's sons
would rather have her tally than any man's on the beach
steers for the skipper's house and has learned the east from it
sits at the slip on idle days and is told what is wrong with every boat but the one he wants
the dealer's house at the river town knows his face and gives him the second-best skins, which is an honour at his age
in the chain's later years he leaves silver over the winter with the host of the Northmen's street on the eastern river, and does not say how much
in the chain's last years a man of the watch on the rock at Birka, whom he beats at the board one year in three
in the chain's later years he pays for the skald's evening question with the news of the east, and has not yet answered one
in the chain's later years he sits at Gairvid's slip on idle days, and is told what is wrong with every boat but the one he wants

lines.greet: You are the Frisian from the Rhine. They say your river sells blades and glass. I know a river that buys them. We should talk, you and I.
lines.greet_again: Good. I hoped it was your sail. I have been counting what a ship would hold, and I need someone to tell me I counted wrong.
rumour: My uncle Hegbjorn went east thirty summers and I never saw him spend an ounce. I mean to spend mine on oak and rivets.
A sword from your country buys more in the east than a boatload of our combs. I have seen it weighed, and seen the seller smile.
Old Vivil says a ship is a hole in the water. I said a hole in the ground does not come home either. He did not like that.
lines.saying: Silver that floats comes back with company.
lines.farewell: Fair wind. When you are next on the Rhine, ask what they give for dark marten. Ask twice. Then tell only me.

people.source: invented, for the chain dirham_hoard: he steers the ship of the ending 'Silver that floats' and is the partner of unlock_partner_ottar. That he is of the Aikgard kin and nephew to the dead Hegbjorn follows the chain's words; how near he stands to Vivil the chain does not say (?). Alive in whatever year the chain is played (805 to 949). Name: Ottar, on a Gotland stone, G 113 (later). Partnership in one purse, the félag, is on rune stones of the 11th century and is used earlier here as the chain does (?).

people.name: Liknat
people.trait: The Gotlanders' skald, such as a people of farmers keeps: he works his own land by day, and each evening asks one question of whoever sits in the shelter above the beach.
people.want: Somebody on this beach who can answer. Failing that, somebody who will carry a question to a place where it can be answered, and come back and say.
people.fear: That the stick he keeps will be put back under a keel, where the wright says it belongs, and a chain of questions end as a charm against rot.
people.voice: Slow, with long silences he does not fill. Grunts for yes. Gives a riddle the way other men give the time of day.
people.looks: An old man by 890, lean and brown, white hair tied back, a farmer's undyed tunic with a good blue cloak over it, a rune-cut stick dark with tar on one side laid across his knees.
knows: the second question of the chain that begins before the Svear king's bench, and where the third is kept
the old riddles of the island, one for each evening of a summer
which boats are home from the east and which are late
what every Gotlander says of the farmer in the north-east who sleeps on silver, and that each names a different farmer
that the Svear king's skald is afraid of boats

ties.note: the Svear king's skald sends men to him for the second stick and has never come himself, being afraid of boats; Liknat says so in every harbour
the host of the big house on the eastern river keeps the third stick for a week's unpaid ale; they send each other whoever can answer, and have never met
the wright had the stick under a keel as a charm against rot and wants it back; the skald says the boat was well tarred
in the chain's later years the steersman pays for an evening's question with the news of the east
of old Likbjorn the stone-cutter's line, three generations on; the riddles came down with the first half of the name

lines.greet: Each evening I ask one, and nobody on this beach answers. Sit. Tonight's is as old as I am, and I did not make it.
lines.greet_again: You came back. Have you an answer, or only another harbour's guess? Sit either way. A guess is more than I get here.
rumour: The stick lay under a keel some winters, as a charm against rot. The boat did not rot. The wright wants it back. I say: good tar.
Every Gotlander will tell you a farmer in the north-east sleeps on more silver than a king eats off. Every Gotlander will tell you it is another farmer.
The Svear king's poet made a chain of questions round the whole sea, and has never been round it. He is afraid of boats. You will know him.
lines.saying: A question is a boat. Somebody has to take it out, or it rots on the beach.
lines.farewell: Go east with it. The river town has the next. Say the Gotlander sent you, and pay for your own ale.

people.source: invented: the 'skald of the Gotlanders' with whom riddles_793.json places r-gest-08 (Paviken, from 871, set dellings_door; Heidreks gatur 8, the leek), and the Gotlanders' skald of the story paviken.dellings_door; uppsalir.arnfast's tie has the stick lying at the slip as a charm against rot, which is how he came by it. The Spillings silver (youngest coin 870/871) is the hoard every Gotlander 'knows' of; nobody on the beach says whose farm. Name: Liknat, on the Gotland rune stone G 113. A skald asks his evening question in the shelter in every later generation.

people.name: Gairvid
people.trait: The wright at the old slip two lifetimes after Rodbjorn, and of his line: he builds the broad Gotland boat as it was always built, and distrusts whatever was not under a keel when he was a boy.
people.want: Seasoned oak, which the island is short of; and his rune stick back under a keel, where it kept the rot off for more winters than he can prove.
people.fear: A dry summer and a spark in the boat sheds; and that his sons will build long and narrow, like Danes.
people.voice: Short sentences, most of them about wood. Knocks on a plank and listens before he answers anything.
people.looks: Broad and stooped, forearms scarred with old pitch burns, a leather apron, wood shavings in a grey beard, an adze with a haft worn to the shape of his hand.
knows: what is wrong with your boat, by the sound of her strakes
what a keel, a strake of oak and a hundred rivets cost on the island this year
the riddle of the big one that wades in the deep, which is sold at this slip with every mending
which houses on the shore sent boats east, and which boats came home sitting low
who took the rune stick from under the keel, and what he was told when he asked for it back

ties.note: his father's father, who laid this slip and sold an anchor riddle with every mending; the riddle is still three pennies' weight
the skald has the rune stick that lay under his keels and will not give it back; no boat rotted while it lay there
the Svear king's skald came off the sea sick at this slip and left a stick for the mending of his boat; the wright took it for a charm and the skald for a question
mends the boat of the amber-cutter's house at the lake of the Este each second summer, and is paid in beads (?)
his house buys her cloth each autumn at the river mouth in Skane, and tells her nothing about its silver
in the chain's later years the steersman sits at the slip on idle days and is told what is wrong with every boat but the one he wants

lines.greet: A Frisian bottom. Flat, and too many nails in her. Haul her up and I will tell you what else, for nothing. Mending costs.
lines.greet_again: She still floats. Then somebody listened to me. Sit on the keel there, not on the strakes; they are drying.
rumour: I had a stick under my keels that kept the rot off. A man with a blue cloak has it now, and asks it questions. Sticks do not answer.
A Svea poet came in here green from the sea and paid for his mending with a stick of runes. I have had worse silver.
Oak is dear. The Danes send theirs to kings. We build broad because we carry sheep and silver, and neither likes to be wet.
lines.saying: A boat tells you everything. You only have to knock.
lines.farewell: Keep her tarred. A charm is a fine thing, but tar is tar.

people.source: invented: the 'paviken.wright' of the ties of uppsalir.arnfast (the second stick of Delling's door, kept at a slip as a charm against rot) and truso.asfrid (a Gute who mends the house's boat); the wright at Rodbjorn's slip in the later 800s. Boat-menders are shown by the rivets and nails all over the working ground, and the working of the shore went on into the 900s (dossier paviken). Name: Gair- + -vid, both on Gotland rune stones (?). The anchor riddle is riddles_793.json r-gest-06.

stories.title: The weight, not the name
stories.summary: On this beach nobody will take the king's penny for what the king says it is. A smith weighs it, nicks it, and tells the merchant what he is carrying. The merchant can learn the scale here, or go on being paid short in every harbour north of the Eider.
stories.picture: The weighing shore in low evening light: a lean smith with burnt forearms holding a small folding balance up against the water, one Frankish penny in the pan, a foreign merchant watching the beam, beads and combs spread on a hide between them.

beats.when: moored and port.id = paviken and not flag.sv_scale
beats.text: You offer pennies by count. The seller looks at them, then at you, then calls the smith. Hegvisl puts one on his pan and a lead weight on the other. He does not look at the king's name.

beats.when: moored and port.id = paviken and not flag.sv_scale
beats.text: He nicks the edge with his knife and bends it on his thumbnail. Good silver, he says, and heavier than the old kind. He offers to pour you a set of weights and show you the beam, for raw glass or for silver by weight.
Sigimar the moneyer sees the nick in your pennies and asks who has been cutting the king's coin. When you say it was weighed, he asks what it weighed. He writes the answer down.
Holmfast weighs your silver twice and once more, sees your own balance come out of its case, and stops at twice. It is as near to a compliment as he comes.
A skipper home from the east pays you in thin white pieces with writing all round and no face. With the scale you know what you hold. Without it you would have taken his word.
On the Curonian shore two men weigh your silver on two beams and get two numbers. With a balance of your own on the plank, and weights neither of them poured, there is a third.
At the lake of the Este the Dane hands the old light pennies back with one finger and takes the new heavy ones as silver. Your scale and his agree. He looks as if he had expected worse of a Frisian.

endings.how: You paid Hegvisl for weights and let him teach the beam, the nick and the bend.
endings.text: You leave with a folding balance in a bronze case and eight lead weights in a bag. Ravn nods once. Aldger says a king's penny was good enough for his father. On the next beach nobody calls a smith.
endings.reward: The thread's flag sv_scale: northern buyers stop shorting the house; weigh_silver and test_silver cost nothing at Paviken; Hegvisl friendly.

endings.how: You brought him raw glass from the Rhine or from the Danes' market and paid for the lesson with it.
endings.text: He turns the cubes over in the light for a long time before he says anything. Then he pours your weights from his own bronze and files each one against his father's set, which he has not done for a stranger before.
endings.reward: sv_scale, the weights filed true (never doubted at any northern market), Hegvisl a fast friend, and first choice of his beads each summer at a fifth under the shore's price.

endings.how: You said a penny is a penny and went on paying by count.
endings.text: They take your pennies, each one weighed against the lightest in the bag. You are not cheated. You are simply paid what the worst of them is worth, on this beach and on every other where there is no king.
endings.reward: Nothing lost but a tenth or so on every northern bargain, until the house learns the scale somewhere: at Ripa, at Helgo, or here on a later call.

stories.reward: The scale and the knowledge that goes with it: the key to every market where silver has no name.

stories.title: The hoard at Aikgard
stories.summary: A Gotland east-farer dies in a western harbour and tells a stranger where his silver lies. On the island his brother holds the farm and his daughter is his only child; each knows half and claims all. The merchant is the only witness, and only he may know of the second lot under the stern stone of an old ship of stones.
stories.picture: A storehouse with its floor boards stacked against the wall: a bronze bowl of arm rings and thin cut coins in a hole under a lifted slab, a heavy farmer kneeling on one side, a young widow standing on the other, neighbours in the doorway, the merchant with a balance.

beats.text: In a western harbour a Gotlander named Hegbjorn is dying of a fever among strangers. He speaks of his farm Aikgard and of twelve feet from the storehouse door toward the tall stone.

beats.when: moored and port.id = paviken and flag.ch_dirham_hoard_1
beats.text: The shipwright puts down his adze before he answers. The brother holds the farm, up the stream past the second ford. The daughter lives under three ash trees nearer the shore, and asks her uncle for nothing.

beats.when: moored and port.id = paviken and flag.ch_dirham_hoard_4
beats.text: Vivil sets bread and ale before you. Ailikn sits by the door with her boy. You must say it to one, to the other, or aloud to both.

beats.when: moored and port.id = paviken and flag.ch_dirham_hoard_5
beats.text: The slab comes up. Fifteen marks, where the dead man spoke of forty less one. Someone must weigh it aloud, and the only stranger present has a scale.

beats.when: moored and port.id = paviken and flag.ch_dirham_hoard_6
beats.text: After the hay the thing meets on the slope above the farms. An old man who knows the law by heart asks who heard the dead man speak, and every head turns to the Frisian.

beats.when: moored and port.id = paviken and flag.ch_dirham_hoard_8
beats.text: The rest lies an arm deep on the seaward side of the stern stone, and you alone know it. You can tell her, tell him, tell all three and speak of a ship, or say nothing.

If the chain falls in her years, Catla of Birka hears of the widow of Aikgard from a skipper: another woman carrying a dead parent's silver. She sends no advice, only word that it weighs less than one thinks and more than one likes.

endings.how: You told Ailikn where the second lot lay.
endings.text: She has it up before her uncle is awake, weighs it three times and buys a shore strip and half a ship. Vivil digs over half his pasture for nothing, unless she is talked into carrying him a share.
endings.reward: Eight marks (960 d), or half of it and two timbers of marten with peace between them; a factor at Paviken (unlock_factor_paviken), and with the peace the guest right of two farms.

endings.how: You told Vivil: it is his pasture.
endings.text: He digs alone at night without a lamp, pays for the carrying, and lays the rest back in the ground in a place he tells nobody. He lives eleven more winters. It is how such silver really went.
endings.reward: Five marks (600 d), three cakes of wax, and twenty paces of shore for a boat shed (unlock_plot_paviken); Ailikn will not answer your greeting.

endings.how: You said the floor was all you knew, and left the stern stone alone.
endings.text: The turf stays whole. The kin search the farm in vain. If you gave the dead man's rune stick unread to his grandson of four, two farms name you their guest for good.
endings.reward: Five marks (600 d) and the dead man's arm ring, made to a weight and never cut (unlock_heirloom_gute_arm_ring); with the stick given, the guest right of Gotland.

endings.how: You sent for a spade and dug by night.
endings.text: Either you are afloat with the bowl before the east is grey and the whole island knows whose spade it was by evening, or the dog is loosed at the fence. A stranger found digging is worth ten marks here, dead.
endings.reward: As much as nineteen marks and a neck ring every smith in the north would know, and a feud: no Gotlander deals with the house, here or at Birka. Or a third taken in secret, which three of your crew also know.

endings.how: You said every word at the thing, then told all three at the table and proposed a ship.
endings.text: Both lots go into oak and rivets on this beach. Ottar steers, Ailikn tallies, Vivil grumbles and leaves the farm's share in, and a booth with a Frisian's mark over the door stands above the tide line. One of the island's hoards is never laid down.
endings.reward: The richest end: over nine marks of silver, sable, marten and wax (about 1,940 d in all), Ottar as a partner (unlock_partner_ottar) and a shore plot (unlock_plot_paviken). History is changed: flags changed_gotland_hoard_spent and changed_frisians_on_gotland.

stories.reward: Silver by the mark, and what is worth more on this island: a host, a plot of shore, or a partner who sails east every summer.

stories.title: Before Delling's door
stories.summary: From 871 a skald of the Gotlanders sits in the shelter above the beach and passes on a chain of old questions that began in the Svear king's hall. Each answer sends the merchant to another harbour. The last answer names a place: a farm in the north-east of the island, and what lies under a floor there.
stories.picture: The open end of a reed-roofed shelter at dusk: an old man with a rune-cut stick across his knees, firelight on his face, a ring of seated crewmen and a merchant leaning forward, the lagoon dark behind them and the first stars out.

beats.text: The Svear king's skald asks what wonder he saw before Delling's door, and will not hear your answer. He says a man on Gotland keeps the next question, and to take him this one.

beats.when: year >= 871 and moored and port.id = paviken
beats.text: The Gotlanders' skald hears the first question, grunts, and gives you a rune stick with another. He says the answer is not on this island, and that the river town in the east has seen it walk.
At the river town a man who buys furs knows the stick's question and laughs at it. He gives you the third, and says it was first asked on a river among the Danes.
On the Danes' river bank the fourth question is answered by a child before you have finished saying it. The fifth must go back to the hall where the first was asked.

The king's skald hears all five answers in order. He is silent a while. Then he says there is a farm in the north-east of Gotland where a man laid more silver under a floor than a boat could carry, and did not come back for it.

beats.when: year >= 871 and moored and port.id = paviken and riddle.r-vafth-52 = solved
beats.text: With five answers given, the skald's boy takes you round the north of the island to a bay with a farm above it. The farmer is a shipowner, his floor is new, and he is at home.

endings.how: You carried every question to its place and gave all five answers at Uppsalir.
endings.text: You are told the place: Spillings, by the bay at Slite, a day and a half round the north of the island from this beach. What you do there, on another man's farm, on an island where your life is priced at ten marks, is your own affair.
endings.reward: rw_hoard_spillings: the place of the greatest silver hoard in the north, as a fetch from Paviken (hoards_793.json spillings); and the standing of a man who can answer in any hall.

endings.how: You answered all five, sailed to the bay, and told the farm's people what the skald said instead of digging.
endings.text: They hear you out at the door and do not ask you in. A year later a boy brings a ring of twisted silver to your boat and says it is for the telling, and that the floor has not been lifted and will not be.
endings.reward: A Gotland arm ring of about 100 g; every Gute feels a little warmer toward the house; and one of history's hoards stays where history found it.

endings.how: You could not answer, or would not sail to four harbours for a riddle.
endings.text: The skald shrugs. The questions are older than he is and will outlast him. He tells one each evening to whoever is in the shelter, and each stick he gives stays in your chest for an heir to try.
endings.reward: The rune sticks themselves (text.t-gest-08 and the others of the set), kept in the chest; the chain can be taken up again by any heir of the house.

stories.reward: The whereabouts of the Spillings silver, or the island's good opinion for leaving it alone.

stories.title: One stone, two shapes
stories.summary: In the 1000s the smith at the stone-walled house casts small silver pendants from one block of sandstone: a hammer if it is hung one way, a cross if it is hung the other. Men come home from the west baptised and want the one; their fathers want the other. A Christian merchant from the Rhine is asked which way up it should hang.
stories.picture: Inside a cold stone-walled store by lamplight: a smith holding a block of yellow sandstone with a T-shaped hollow cut in it, a newly cast silver pendant on his palm, an old farmer with a hammer amulet at his neck and a young skipper with a cross at his, both watching.

beats.when: year >= 1000 and moored and port.id = paviken
beats.text: The smith shows you the stone. He pours, waits, and tips out a bright shape with a short stem and two arms. He holds it stem down, then stem up. He says he sells more of them this way.

beats.when: year >= 1008 and moored and port.id = paviken
beats.text: A skipper home from England has had water poured on him there. He wants a priest brought to the island, quietly, and asks whether a Frisian boat has room for a man with a book.
At the Danes' west market a priest hears of the stone and laughs until he coughs. Then he asks how many crosses the man sells, and says that is how it began here too.

beats.when: year >= 1008 and moored and port.id = paviken
beats.text: The old farmers have heard. Nobody threatens you. One says that a wooden house for the new god was burnt on this island not long ago, and that it was a pity about the timber.
The bishop in the Svear king's new town has heard that the Gotlanders pour hammers and crosses from one stone. He does not laugh. He asks how many of each, and has the answer written down.

endings.how: You said it was not your stone and bought some of each.
endings.text: The smith goes on pouring. Hammers go east and crosses go west out of the same hollow, and he weighs both on the same pan. Your crew wear what they like under their shirts, as they always have.
endings.reward: Pendants at the smith's own price (brooches in the hold, wanted at Birka's heirs and among the Danes); no feeling lost with anyone on the beach.

endings.how: You carried a priest from the Danes' market to the outlet quays as a passenger.
endings.text: He is lodged on the skipper's farm and says Mass in a barn. Some come. Nobody burns the barn, this time. The old farmers are cool to you for a year and then forget, because your prices are fair.
endings.reward: The baptised skippers of the island as fast friends and buyers; a good name with the bishops of the Danes and at Bremen (deed: a mission carried); the old farms cool for a season.

endings.how: You said a Frisian boat carries cargo, not quarrels, and left the priest where he was.
endings.text: The young skipper shrugs and finds another boat the next summer. The old farmer who spoke of the burnt timber sends a cheese to your shelter and says nothing with it.
endings.reward: The old farms a little warmer, the host's good word, and a standing welcome at the ring of stones: an oath sworn there by the house is taken without a second witness.

stories.reward: Friends on one side of the island's slow change of faith, or the rarer thing: none lost on either.

stories.title: Gold shut in glass
stories.summary: The bead-maker in the walled yard works with small bright cubes of glass that come north through many hands. The best have a leaf of gold shut inside. He does not know they are prised from the walls of old churches in the south, and when he is told, he does not mind. He wants more, and a boat from the Rhine can bring them.
stories.picture: The walled yard at midday: a long hearth, a clay platform with rows of small red, yellow and blue glass cubes, a smith turning an iron rod in the flame with a bead growing on it, a merchant holding one gold-flecked cube up to the sun.

beats.text: Hegvisl shows you a cube no bigger than a fingernail, with gold inside the glass. He has nine. He asks where they are made. You have seen such things before, small and far up, in a church wall.

The bead-makers on the Danes' west market buy the same cubes by the bag from Frisians. They say the bags come down the Rhine, and before that over mountains, and that the seller never says from where.

On the Rhine strand a man sells broken glass by weight for melting. Under the cullet in his basket are bright cubes with mortar still on them. He says an old wall fell down, somewhere south, and looks at the river.

beats.when: moored and port.id = paviken and hold.raw_glass >= 1
beats.text: You tip the bag onto his clay platform. He sorts them by colour without speaking, the gold ones last. You tell him what wall they came from. He says a bead is seen more often than a wall.
Ragnvi of Birka gets the same bright cubes, fewer and dearer, and has never had one with gold in it. Hegvisl sends her his failed colours to guess at. She would rather he sent a gold one.
On the eastern river the bead-maker turns a gold cube over once and hands it back. Gold shut in glass buys nothing in the woods, she says. An eye does.

endings.how: You brought raw glass north and sold it to the yard.
endings.text: From then on the yard keeps its first strings for your boat. Somewhere on a river in the east a woman wears a bead that was once part of a saint's robe, and nobody between here and there knows it but you.
endings.reward: A standing buyer for raw glass at Paviken at a third over the Rhine price, and beads bought at source a fifth under the shore's: a small steady run that pays every call.

endings.how: You sold him the bag but kept the gold cubes back, and gave them to a church at home.
endings.text: Aldger carries them ashore in his cap. The priest sets them in the wax round a candle on the altar and asks no questions either. Hegvisl says you have odd ideas about what glass is for, and pays for the rest.
endings.reward: The same buyer, a little cooler; a good deed with the church at home (alms); and Aldger's morale, which is not a small thing on a long voyage.

endings.how: You sold the glass at the Danes' west market instead.
endings.text: A fair price and a shorter voyage. On your next call the walled yard has amber and garnet on the platform and no bright glass at all, and the smith does not look up from the fire.
endings.reward: Silver now; the Ripa bead-makers friendly; Hegvisl answers shortly until glass is brought to him.

stories.reward: A trade of your own that no toll touches: glass north, beads and knowledge back.

works.name: A hauling way of oak rollers
works.what: Split oak logs bedded across the dragging hollow from the water's edge to above the tide line, with a post and a rope of walrus hide to haul against. The beach's own work, done with the farm's leave and the wright's eye.
works.needs: Rodiaud's farm at least easy with the house, and the shipwright of the day willing to set the line.
works.gives: Hauling out and careening here take half the hands and half the days for this house, and the wright looks at her bottom for nothing each time she comes up.
works.picture: A shingle beach with a worn hollow running up from still water, pale split logs laid across it like the rungs of a ladder, six men hauling a clinker boat up them on a rope, a shipwright watching with an adze on his shoulder.
works.source: invented in the period's manner; the hollow worn by dragging boats is found (Gotland Archaeological Field School, 'Paviken'). Rollers and a hauling post are the ordinary way (?).

works.name: A boat shed on the shore strip
works.what: A long narrow shed of posts, wattle and turf on twenty paces of a farm's shore, open at the water end, where a boat can lie dry through the winter with her gear hung from the rafters.
works.needs: A plot of shore: given before neighbours by a farm (the chain's unlock_plot_paviken), or the standing word of a host who answers for the house. No outlander can simply buy ground here.
works.gives: A winter berth on Gotland: the boat may be laid up here and the house may sail from here in spring, weeks ahead of any boat coming from the west; stores a boatload dry.
works.picture: A low turf-roofed shed open toward a frozen lagoon, the stem of a tarred boat showing in its mouth, oars and a rolled sail slung under the rafters, snow on the shingle and smoke from a farm behind.
works.source: works_793.json boat_shed; the shore strip marked with four stones before two neighbours is the chain dirham_hoard's. No foreign merchant is known to have held ground on the island before the 12th century (?): the game says so and makes it hard.

works.name: A picture stone for one who sailed
works.what: A slab of limestone taller than a man, narrow at the neck and wide at the head, cut and painted: at the foot a ship under a chequered sail with her crew, above it a rider met by a woman with a horn. The ship is cut from yours.
works.needs: A dead man of the house, the crew or the partnership to remember, and the carver on the slope at least easy with you.
works.gives: As a rune stone: the dead man is remembered by name in the house's book and by the crew; and the Gutes count the house among those who know how things are done.
works.picture: A tall keyhole-shaped slab of pale stone on a grassy slope above a lagoon, a red and black ship under a chequered sail cut at its foot and a rider above, a thin old carver stepping back from it with a mallet, a boat's crew standing bareheaded.
works.source: story/unlocks_793.json memorial_picture_stone (300 d, 40 days; works_793.json rune_stone); the stones of Tjängvide, Ardre and Lärbro, 8th to 10th century (?); en.wikipedia 'Picture stone'. None is recorded from Paviken itself (dossier 6).

works.name: A berth at the new quays
works.what: Six oak piles and a run of planking added to the quays at the outlet, with the house's mark cut in the head of the end pile. The men who built the quays in 1008 let others add to them for a price.
works.needs: A call in or after 1008, and a Gotland farm that will speak for the house: a host, a factor or a partner.
works.gives: The house can still load deep here when the old beach takes only small boats; loading takes a day less. A spring flood may carry it away, as it did the rest: then it must be paid for again or given up.
works.picture: Two rows of new oak piles with planking at a stream mouth, a laden trading ship afloat alongside, men driving a pile with a heavy maul, a curved earth bank rising behind them and a line of pile heads in the water beyond.
works.source: Timber quays and jetties at the outlet, tree-ring dated to 1008 and wrecked by a spring flood (Gotland Archaeological Field School, 'Paviken'; sv.wikipedia 'Västergarnsvallen'). That a stranger could pay for a stretch is invented (?).

ships.how: bought second-hand on the beach, or built to order over a winter
ships.note: The boat of every farm on this coast, close kin to the house's own: clinker-built, four or five pairs of oars, a small square sail, light enough to drag. The slip always has one that an east-farer's widow wants sold.
ships.picture: A slim tarred clinker boat on rollers on pale shingle, a chequered sail folded in her, a broad shipwright knocking on her strakes with his knuckles while a widow with keys at her belt waits.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json norse_small_boat (cultures: gutes); story/ships_793.json built_at includes paviken; clinker boats with iron rivets (Gotland Archaeological Field School, 'Paviken').
