ships.how: built to order over a winter and a spring, if the owner finds the oak; sometimes bought second-hand from a house whose skipper did not come home
ships.note: The ship the east-farers sail: twelve to eighteen paces of oak and pine, one square sail in chequers of two colours, oars for the rivers. The wright will lay her down if you can wait, and will tell you each visit what you should have asked for instead. After about 1050 the lagoon will not float her.
ships.picture: A half-planked hull on a shingle slip, pale new strakes over dark, rows of rivet heads catching the light, a wright sighting along her with one eye shut, the still lagoon and a narrow gap of sea behind.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json norse_allround_ship (cultures: gutes); story/ships_793.json. Boats were mended here for certain; that ships were built is the usual reading and is not shown by the pages opened (?) (dossier 2, 8). Chequered sails from the picture stones (en.wikipedia 'Picture stone').

sayings.text: Cattle die, and kinsmen die, / And so one dies one's self; / But a noble name will never die, / If good renown one gets.
sayings.source: Hávamál 77, tr. Henry Adams Bellows, The Poetic Edda (1923), as given in Design/content/lore/proverbs_jokes.json pj019. What the carver says while he cuts.

sayings.text: To question and answer must all be ready / Who wish to be known as wise; / Tell one thy thoughts, but beware of two, / All know what is known to three.
sayings.source: Hávamál 63, tr. Bellows 1923 (proverbs_jokes.json pj015). The island's rule about silver, and the reason three crewmen knowing is a cost.

sayings.text: He welcomes the night whose fare is enough, / (Short are the yards of a ship,) / Uneasy are autumn nights; / Full oft does the weather change in a week, / And more in a month's time.
sayings.source: Hávamál 74, tr. Bellows 1923 (proverbs_jokes.json pj145). Said on the beach when the east-farers are late.

sayings.text: Forth shall one go, nor stay as a guest / In a single spot forever; / Love becomes loathing if long one sits / By the hearth in another's home.
sayings.source: Hávamál 35, tr. Bellows 1923 (proverbs_jokes.json pj009). The host's way of saying the wind has turned.

sayings.text: We asked to stay only for the waxing and waning of the moon. Later we explained that this means for ever.
sayings.source: The Gotlanders who went to the land of the Greeks, in the Guta saga (about 1220, late); our own plain retelling, not a translation, as in peoples/svea_gotlandic.md 9. Told here by a Gute against his own people.

sayings.text: Silver has one name, and it is its weight.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the practice from the spine (silver_road) and economy/silver_coin.md

sayings.text: The Frank counts his silver, the Svea weighs it, and the Gute buries it. Ask the Gute which of them sleeps.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; a turn on the saying in places/helgo.json, as a Gotlander would answer it

sayings.text: A hole in the ground has never been lost off the Curonian shore.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner (a Gotlander's understatement); Vivil's line in this file

sayings.text: No toll man, no king, no wall. We have to be honest. It is very tiring.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; no ruler or toll is recorded for the harbour (dossier 1, 4)

easter_eggs.text: The small bright cubes on the bead-maker's platform were cut to make pictures of saints on church walls in Italy. On this beach they are melted, a few at a time, into beads for women who have never heard of either.
easter_eggs.source: Opaque glass cubes, mosaic tesserae read as Italian, among the raw glass (Gotland Archaeological Field School, 'Paviken'; dossier 4, 7). The gold-in-glass kind is known from other northern workshops; here it is the game's guess (?)

easter_eggs.text: Under the hollow where the boats are dragged lies a man with nothing beside him and no stone over him. Every keel on the beach passes above him. Nobody now alive can say who he was, and the wright steps a little wide at that place without knowing why.
easter_eggs.source: A burial in the boat-dragging hollow at the waterfront, with no grave goods and no marker, poorly recorded (Gotland Archaeological Field School; dossier 2, 7). Its date is not given: that it is older than 793 is the game's guess (?)

easter_eggs.text: One low heap on the slope is twice as long as the others. A man lies there with his horse and his dog, so that he need not walk and need not walk alone.
easter_eggs.source: A grave in the south grave field holding a dog and a horse (Gotland Archaeological Field School; dossier 2, 6)

easter_eggs.text: The block of sandstone on the ledge has one shape cut in it: a short stem and two arms. Poured and hung stem down it is a hammer. Hung stem up it is a cross. The smith has not decided which it is, and has not been asked to.
easter_eggs.source: A sandstone mould for crosses or Thor's hammers from the stone-walled house, dug 1995 (Gotland Archaeological Field School; dossier 2, 6, 7)

easter_eggs.text: A thumb-long bar of gold is lost somewhere in the ash of the working ground and never missed enough to be looked for. It will lie there until 2013, when it turns up in the heap of earth that an earlier dig had already searched and thrown away.
easter_eggs.source: A small gold bar found in the old spoil in 2013 (Gotland Archaeological Field School; dossier 7)

easter_eggs.text: The harbour is sealed twice. In the early 1000s its own people shut the entrance with a row of piles. In the 1970s the people who dug it lay a black sheet over the floor they have not reached, and forty years on it is found whole.
easter_eggs.source: The pile row (sv.wikipedia 'Paviken'); the black plastic laid in the 1970s and found intact in 2013 (Gotland Archaeological Field School; dossier 7)

easter_eggs.text: Two hundred years after this beach's first Frisian, brothers on this island raise a painted stone for a man named Ravn, dead far to the south before a river fall called Aifor. Among the brothers is a Hegbjorn, and the man who gave the order was a Vivil.
easter_eggs.source: The Pilgårds stone, G 280, about 950 to 1000 (?) (runes_793.json pilgards_g280). The game's crewman Ravn and the chain's Hegbjorn and Vivil take their names from it; they are not those men

easter_eggs.text: Nobody on the beach calls it Paviken. They say 'the bay', or 'on the bay'. What the Gotlanders of these years called their harbour was never written down.
easter_eggs.source: The name is modern, said to come from 'pa viken', 'on the bay'; older maps call the water Västergarnsviken (sv.wikipedia 'Paviken', after Lundström; dossier 1)

easter_eggs.text: More than half the bone in the rubbish pits is cattle. Other harbours live on fish and pig. Here the men who work the hearths are farmers first, and they eat like it.
easter_eggs.source: 65 per cent of the studied bone is cattle, unlike other harbours, though only 3 per cent of the bone was studied (Gotland Archaeological Field School; dossier 4)

easter_eggs.text: In the reeds at the stream mouth there are fat golden carp as long as a man's forearm, which nobody troubles to catch while there is cod. A thousand years on, the lagoon is a lake, and the carp and the birds have it to themselves.
easter_eggs.source: Today the lake is a bird reserve of some 240 species, known for giant crucian carp (en.wikipedia and sv.wikipedia 'Paviken'; dossier 7). That the carp were there in these years is the game's guess (?)

easter_eggs.text: In the 1030s somebody on the seaward shore wears an English king's penny on a thong, pierced through the king's eye. It was money once, in another country.
easter_eggs.source: An English penny of the 1030s worn as a pendant, lost at Västergarn (sv.wikipedia 'Västergarnsvallen'; dossier 5). The hole through the eye is invented

unlocks.what: A folding balance and a set of northern weights, and the knowing of how to use them
unlocks.how: Let the smith weigh your penny, then pay him in silver by weight or in raw glass for weights of your own (the story 'The weight, not the name').
unlocks.gives: flag sv_scale: buyers north of the Eider stop paying the house by its lightest coin; act:weigh_silver and act:test_silver cost nothing here. Counts toward unlock_heirloom_scales.

unlocks.what: A host on Gotland who answers for the house
unlocks.how: Bring the landing gift to Rodiaud's door yourself on three calls, make no trouble in her shelter, and eat what you are given.
unlocks.gives: Free lodging in the shelter; the house's men are under her farm's protection, so no card of the harbour can cost a life for a stranger's price; she tells you who is in harbour and what they would not say they carried (ask_harbour, sure).

unlocks.what: The shipwright's riddle of the thing that fights wave and wind
unlocks.how: Buy the rune stick from the shipwright for three pennies' weight (text.t-gest-06) and bring him the answer.
unlocks.gives: rw_tip_paviken: the freshest word on Paviken's prices; and the wright looks over your hull for nothing that call.

unlocks.how: Sit with the carver on the slope; he gives two rune sticks for nothing (text.t-gest-35, text.t-vafth-47) to anyone who asks him what the pictures mean.
unlocks.gives: Two texts for the chest with their riddles; answering both makes him a fast friend and takes a fifth off the price of a picture stone.

unlocks.what: A Gotland picture stone for a dead man of the house
unlocks.how: act:remember at the southern graves, with 300 d and forty days (memorial_picture_stone).
unlocks.gives: As a rune stone; inherited; the Gutes count the house among those who know how things are done.
